book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

chapters.file: ch10 - 8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey.md
chapters.relation: Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.

chapters.file: ch11 - 9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom.md
chapters.relation: Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.

chapters.file: ch12 - 10. Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood as Philosophy Children as Philosophers.md
chapters.relation: Baggett argues that Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was a profoundly philosophical show because it treated very young children as natural philosophers — curious, wonder-filled questioners — rather than mere proto-adults. He frames child-development theory through the rationalism/empiricism divide (Skinner's behaviorism descending from Locke's tabula rasa, Chomsky's innatism from Descartes) and champions Gareth Matthews's claim that children's 'romancing' is genuine philosophy adults should not condescend to. Rogers modeled Hadot's philosophy-as-a-way-of-life and James's and Rousseau's active learning; episodes on death (the goldfish), work, and make-believe invited the same wonder Aquinas and Hume brought to happiness and causation, treating children as members of Kant's kingdom of ends.

chapters.file: ch13 - 11. Futurama as Philosophy Wisdom from the Ignorance of a Delivery Boy.md
chapters.relation: Lewis surveys how Futurama's satire raises philosophical questions without taking sides. 'Zoidberg's Freedom Lesson' pits Mill's harm principle and free speech against Feinberg's offense principle; the mutants' and robots' oppression is read through Foucault's disciplinary normalcy and Locke's and Rawls's social contracts (state of nature, veil of ignorance). 'The Problem with Popplers' stages Bentham's utilitarianism, a might-makes-right food-chain view, and an intelligence criterion that commits Singer's 'speciesism,' with sentimentality winning. 'The Late Philip J. Fry' and 'Free Will Hunting' dramatize determinism, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, and Sartre's existentialist free will, while 'Godfellas' and 'A Clockwork Origin' probe the problem of evil, fine-tuning, and Occam's razor.

chapters.file: ch14 - 12. Firefly as Philosophy Social Contracts, Political Dissent, and Virtuous Communities.md
chapters.relation: Kowalski argues that Firefly and Serenity embody a distinctive political theory he calls 'Since I Found Serenity' (SIFS). The mindless, savage Reavers represent Hobbes's state of nature, showing government is necessary; but the Alliance's torture of River, the Miranda/Pax atrocity, and the murderous blue-gloved agents and Operative make a Hobbesian reading untenable and vindicate Locke's natural rights and right of revolution — Mal's 'I aim to misbehave' broadcast of the Miranda file is Lockean civil disobedience. He then presses the tacit-consent problem (the Browncoats cannot leave the 'Verse) and supplements Locke with Aristotle's friendship and community: Serenity's crew becomes a virtuous mobile commonwealth where friendship (Simon forgiving Jayne, Mal's 'love keeps her in the air') turns a commonwealth into a good-life community.

chapters.file: ch15 - 13. Arrested Development as Philosophy Family First What We Owe Our Parents.md
chapters.relation: Phillips uses the dysfunctional Bluths to ask what, if anything, adult children owe their parents. Against Sidgwick's reluctance and various grounds for filial obligation, he argues negatively through the family: George Sr. and Lucille never meet the motivation and above-duty conditions for a debt of gratitude; adopted Lindsay's absentee mothering of Maeby shows biology alone grounds nothing; and Michael's dutiful-son and overbearing-father roles show the social role of 'parent' is not enough (Hardimon's 'reflectively acceptable' roles). Positively, deploying Aristotle's three friendships (utility, pleasure, virtue), he argues that only a voluntary friendship of virtue grounds special obligations — illustrated when a rock-bottom, 'useless' Gob and George Sr. finally bond as near-equals, the show's closest thing to genuine friendship.

chapters.file: ch16 - 14. The Doctor as Philosopher The Collectivist-Realist Pacifism of the Doctor and the Quest for Social Justice.md
chapters.relation: Smithka argues the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist': morally opposed to war yet willing, as a last resort, to use lethal force for social justice. She places the Doctor on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum (past absolute and collectivist pacifism), augmenting it with Martin Luther King Jr.'s realist pacifism — ethical appeals 'undergirded by constructive coercive power' — and Gandhi's ahimsa and belief that no one is beyond redemption (the Doctor sparing Davros, offering enemies a choice). She tests Kant's duty ethics and respect for persons (Rule 1: the Doctor lies), Ross's prima facie duties, Mill's utilitarianism ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Beast Below'), Gilligan/Noddings care ethics, and Wolterstorff's 'life of needs,' and reads 'The Day of the Doctor' as a Rawlsian veil of ignorance brokering Zygon-human peace.

holes.name: The Philosophy of Childhood (children as natural philosophers)
holes.what: The view, associated with Gareth Matthews, that childhood is itself a domain of philosophical inquiry and that young children spontaneously do genuine philosophy before it is schooled out of them.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire thesis is that Mister Rogers treated children as philosophers; no taxonomy slug names the philosophy of childhood or the child-as-philosopher claim it applies to the show.

holes.name: Filial Obligation (what adult children owe their parents)
holes.what: The debated special moral obligations adult children may owe parents, and the candidate grounds for them — indebtedness, gratitude, biology, social role, or friendship.
holes.why: Chapter 13 (numbered 15) is built entirely around the ground of filial obligation and the 'Family First' motto; the taxonomy has friendship and gratitude fragments but no slug for filial/parental obligation itself.

holes.name: Pacifism (the moral opposition to war)
holes.what: The family of positions morally opposing war, ranging from absolute pacifism to collectivist, pragmatic, and realist pacifism on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum.
holes.why: Chapter 14 (numbered 16) argues at length that the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist'; the taxonomy offers just-war-theory and ahimsa but no general slug for pacifism, which is the chapter's central classifying concept.
